title: Part 4
text: she hauled herself up onto the shallow incline and swept the beam back across the black. From here she could keep the light on the others. Maybe make it a little less daunting. “Come on!” Leon went first. He lowered himself in without ceremony, one hand on the wall, keeping his eyes forward and slightly up the way he'd been doing since the hallway. Not looking at the water. Definitely not thinking about the particular quality of dark water, the way it closed over your shoulders like something deciding, the specific cold of a lake in summer that shouldn't have been cold but was— He moved through it efficiently. Hand on the wall, feet finding the floor on the other side, up and out. Simple. Done. David followed slower, sliding into the hole with a soft curse and kicking across it with mechanical rhythm. His limbs felt heavier in the water than they should. He didn’t like it. Didn’t like the silence, or the drag, or the way the space bent around them. But he made it. Dwight whined once, a low pained sound in the depths of his chest, before following David. The water lapped gently at his legs as the others waited on the far side. His hands trembled at his sides, stomach clenching uncomfortably, then settled into a low grumble. The last time he was in there had been absolute hell. Last time the dark had been complete and the water had been warm and patient and something had kept bumping his legs in the— He got in. This time, at least... there were eyes on him. David's hand found his arm on the other side before he'd even asked for it, hauling him up onto solid tile. His whole frame shook as he pulled free from the water. Jake watched the others come up on the far side, dripping and breathing hard, and mentally measured the gap. The pressure in the wall shifted slightly and he side-eyed it for a moment, before tucking the crowbar into his belt and stepping forward. The edge of the tile shifted under his foot. Not dramatically — just a subtle wrongness under his leading foot, the tile angling wrong in a way that registered a half-second too late, then there was no floor. He didn’t even get out a full warning. Just a single, startled “Shit—!” as the water closed over his head and the hole took him. “Jake?!” Orela’s light jerked toward the surface, but it only caught ripples. “Jake!” Dwight moved on pure reflex, already leaning toward the gap before his brain had caught up with what was happening, and Orela's hand caught his arm and yanked him back hard enough to stagger him. "Don't—" He froze. Teetered. The edge was gone again. “He’s not... he was right there!” David was already stepping forward. "I'll get him—" "No—!" The word came out of Dwight sharper than he'd intended, sharp enough to stop David mid-step. He didn't know where it came from. He just knew, with a certainty that sat in his chest like something physical, that David going back into that water was not something he could let happen. Orela’s jaw clenched. She shoved her flashlight into Leon’s hands, voice low and steady even as her knuckles shook. "David’s injured. You’re the faster swimmer out of us. You’ve got the best chance. Find him." Leon stared at the light for half a second too long, then down at the black water yawning in front of him. His jaw tightened. The universe, he thought, had a very specific and deeply personal sense of humor. Of course it would be him. It was just his luck. He'd prevented the end of the world more times than he could count on one hand and apparently the lesson the cosmos had taken from that was this guy can handle anything, let's keep testing it. The lake water surfaced briefly in the back of his mind and he put it down. He obviously wasn’t going to leave Jake behind. He handed Orela his vest, checked his grip on the flashlight, took a few steadying breaths, dove clean, and vanished beneath the surface. The darkness swallowed the beam almost immediately. The others watched the light sink below the surface and disappear, and then there was nothing. Just the water lapping softly at the edge of the hole and five people minus one standing very still in the dark. Nobody moved. The floor had already demonstrated what it thought about people who moved. Dwight counted his own heartbeats and tried not to think about the last time he'd been waiting for someone to come back up through a hole in the floor. That time everything had happened fast, the water rising, the clock obvious and urgent. This was slower. The waiting stretched and the dark pressed in and slow, it turned out, was its own particular kind of terrible. David cursed gently to himself, trying to calm the reflexive itch in his lungs. Dwight's outcry rang sharp in his mind, and for a moment he was back in the basement; lost, panicked, flailing at everything rhythm touched him. Dwight had nearly lost him down there, and he just tried to go right back in without even thinking. His own bull-headed reflexes were causing pain on others. They were already scared enough. He needed to get them out before it got worse. Orela stared at the spot where she had last seen the light and tried not to second guess herself. Leon had gone in reluctantly — she'd seen it, the particular quality of his hesitation, something underneath the pragmatism that he wasn't going to name and she wasn't going to ask about. He seemed to be struggling with something beyond just the darkness and the rising threat. The man clearly had baggage; Orela had seen that look before. She didn't know him that well, he wasn't really one to open up about his time before the Fog, but if something down there triggered an episode in him, it could be extremely bad for everyone. Beyond it all, though, was a single shared understanding. If Leon didn't come back, they were down two people and their only light source. The water lapped softly at the edge of the hole. The basement was unrecognizable. Leon’s hands found the pipe just beneath the surface and clung to it hard. He didn’t kick — didn’t fight the current — just pulled himself forward along the ceiling, trying to save energy while he searched. The basement was wrong. The entire area was foreign — somehow both too small and too large at once — swollen and warped out of shape in unnatural, unrecognizable configurations. But the pressure folded in all the same. Columns were shattered. Furniture drifted like corpses. Concrete sheared open. Rebar jutted like bones from a ribcage halfway through collapse. The flashlight cut maybe four feet in any direction before the water swallowed it. Everything beyond that was shadow. The shadows kept looking like people. He grabbed at one — fabric, he'd thought, or an arm, or something — and his knuckles came back scraped against broken concrete. He grabbed at another and found a shelf corner. He stopped grabbing at shadows. Something had settled down here. That was the feeling of it — not abandoned, not empty, but claimed. The debris wasn't random the way one might expect from a flood. It had the quality of accumulation, of things drawn in and kept. The current moved through it in slow deliberate patterns that didn't quite match the angles of the space. He pushed deeper, ears roaring, light darting in frantic sweeps. Come on, Jake. Where are you? The dark lake water surfaced briefly at the back of his mind. The pressure of something large moving beneath— He pulled himself forward along the next pipe. Found the next one. Kept moving. He hauled forward one grip at a time, flashlight clamped in his fist, beam darting through the water like a scalpel. The current tugged hard now. Not enough to sweep him outright, but enough to throw him off course with every pull. He gritted his teeth, adjusted, and kept going. Shapes moved below him. Pale smears and dark shadows. He kicked once to steer around a floating chair and nearly slammed his shin into what might’ve been a filing cabinet. The pain lanced through his leg, and he winced tight against it, familiar panic sparking in the back of his throat. He forced it down. Focus. Focus. He swept the light again. Leon saw the movement first — a disturbance in the water below him, too deliberate for current, too rhythmic for debris — and angled the flashlight down. The Entity's claws had come through the floor. Not violently. Not dramatically. They'd simply grown there, pushing up through the concrete like roots push through a sidewalk — patient and inevitable and completely indifferent to what the floor thought about it. Three of them visible in the beam, dark and articulated and wrong in the specific way that things with too many joints were wrong. One of them had Jake. Not aggressively. That was the thing that made it worse. The claw had hooked itself into the fabric of his pant leg and was tugging — gently, almost playfully, letting him rise up a bit before smoothly sinking him again. Jake flailed violently against it, twisting, eyes wide, limbs kicking at what he had assumed was floating trash. He had been fighting something he couldn't see, and now that the light had found him, the shift in him was immediate and total. The stressed tension of I’m caught on something became the flailing panic of I can see what has me and those were completely different animals. Leon kicked sharp off the wall. He dropped fast, grabbing Jake around the torso, one arm clamping across his ribs as the other jammed the flashlight into the crook of his elbow as Jake grabbed at his arm, trying to climb him to freedom. He kicked down hard past Jake at the claw, connecting sharply along the edge. It flexed but held. Leon kicked again, striking where the claw curled. Jake screamed something underwater — more air bubbles than sound — as the tension tightened. The claw flinched sharply, ripping into the pant leg and almost tugging Jake out of Leon’s arms. He aimed another kick down, and another. The tip of the claw split, a shard slicing through Jake’s leg as the rest recoiled. The cut bloomed scarlet, the water drinking it fast. Jake thrashed, twisting hard against Leon's hold. The other claws lashed out immediately, reaching, trying to reclaim their prize. No time. Leon turned, twisting upward, dragging Jake through the chaos and out of range of the Entity’s claws. Jake was half-kicking, half-flailing, trying to help, but his strength was gone and his leg wouldn't move right. Leon could feel it — the dead weight setting in. His own limbs burned. His lungs were screaming. But the light still worked, and that beam led them cleanly up, sputtering bright against the ceiling until, at last, it found the edges of the gap. He never bothered looking back to see if the claws were following. In his mind, they were already reaching out for him from the dark. His fingers found the pipe again and dragged. He didn't look back. The hole was where he'd left it. They surfaced in a violent crash — Jake bursting first in a flailing panic, Leon a heartbeat behind, his shoulder cracking sharp against the tile. Chests heaving. Coughing. Gagging up water between breaths that tasted like blood and mold with enough force that if they had the breath for it, they would have surfaced screaming. The others were already there — Orela's hands finding Jake's arm, Dwight surging forward after a single paralyzed breath of relief. Leon collapsed half into the hallway, half into the water, David catching him by the back of the shirt and pulling him fully onto the tile before he slid back in. “Hey — hey, I got you,” he muttered, bracing his weight and firmly thumping his back as Leon choked on another mouthful of water and shuddered violently. He held him steady until the spasms passed. “You’re one lucky bastard, you know that?” Jake coughed so hard he nearly vomited. He sagged into Orela’s hold as he caught his breath. “She moved the fucking floor.” His voice had a quality to it that hadn't been there before — stripped of the arrogant edge it had earlier, raw underneath. "I felt it shift. I knew She was in the building and I stepped on it anyway and She just—" He stopped. "It was just playing with me. It had me and it was just—" "It’s ok. You're out," Orela ran her hand over his leg, assessing the cut with quick professional focus. “It’s not deep, Messy, but not deep. You’ll be fine, so long as whatever’s in this water doesn’t give you a random infection.” Jake looked at the hole. At the water lapping at its edge with that same patient quality it had had all night. “I’ve had worse,” Jake muttered, wiping his face and wincing as Orela tied his bandana around the cut, slowing the bleed to a more reasonable level. Dwight stared at them both, still breathing too fast as anxiety clamped around him. David kept a hand on Leon’s shoulder, not to steady him anymore — but to ground himself. The hallway fell into a quiet tension. Just the sound of their breath. The creak of the building. And the water lapping, steady as ever, just behind them. From the classroom doorway, Danny’s phone caught everything; the thrash of the beam below water, the long, terrifying silence, the sudden eruption of two soaked survivors clawing back to life. He zoomed in, framed it perfectly. On the RC feed from his submersible, the lens had tracked them the whole way, Jake’s bubbles scattering, Leon’s frantic dive, the scramble back to air. A perfect double angle. Danny chuckled low into his mask, whispering like a delighted commentator. "And there it is, back from the brink. Lucky boys. She’s playing with you now! Better get a move on." He zoomed in. Framed it. Waited. Ch 7 – Floodgate The back door was worse than the front. That shouldn't have been possible. The front door had been a wall wearing a door's memory — swollen past function, the frame warped into something that had forgotten what gaps were for. But this one had gone further, past bloated and into something that looked almost geological. The wood had darkened to near-black, grain split in long weeping lines, the surface slick and soft in places where it had absorbed so much water it had stopped being wood in any meaningful sense. The metal was gone entirely — hinges, handle, strike plate, all of it reduced to rust-colored suggestions fused permanently to the frame. Even the seam where door met wall had disappeared, the entire frame curled outward like it had been soaking for decades. David hit it anyway. Shoulder first, weight behind it, the impact landing with that same swallowed quality that everything in this building produced — force going in, nothing coming back. Leon followed with a length of shelving, the metal edge finding no purchase on a surface too soft to catch and too solid to dent. Jake worked the bottom with his boot, then his knee, then his boot again. The water climbed past their hips and shifted with every impact, sloshing back against their legs like a rebuttal. The crowbar was gone. Somewhere in the hallway, or the particular pocket of dark water that had taken Jake and had likely kept what fell out of his hands as a consolation prize. They were down to bodies and debris, and the door received both with the same patient indifference. Dwight had his back to the wall, arms wrapped tight against himself. His eyes kept flicking down to the water creeping up his legs, the anxiety sucking at his ribs. The flow had quieted — not stagnant, but sluggish — dragged thin across the endless sprawl of the building. It left behind a slick murk clinging to corners, swallowing dropped tools and broken tile alike. It crawled up the grout — slow but certain. He watched it tick past a screw left embedded in the tile. Then past a crack in the plaster. His lips moved again, quieter, a whisper under his breath. "Five... there’s five of us. There shouldn’t be five." The others didn’t notice, too caught in the rhythm of smashing and straining. Their grunts filled the hallway. The sharp clang of a metal desk leg on rotted wood. The curse of another wasted swing. But Dwight’s eyes were wide, haunted, thoughts spiraling. “Four survivors,” he whispered. “Two gates. Four skills. Two exits. Always balance. Always ritual. The Entity loved symmetry. So why...” He trailed off. Five people. His lips moved silently, mumbling, counting. Five. It’s never five. Why? The question chased its own tail. He pressed his palm flat against the wall behind him, feeling the damp of it, and tried to find the shape of what was nagging at him. The math was ruthless but it was clean. It accounted for everyone. Five didn't account for everyone. His eyes moved across the group without meaning to, cataloguing. David. Leon. Jake. Orela. Is one of us not meant to— He didn't finish the thought. Pressed it back down, hard, and fixed his gaze on the door like that would help. Down the hall, Danny had found himself a perch. The cabinet had toppled at some point during the building's ongoing renovation of itself, landing at an angle against the wall that made it serviceable enough — one knee pulled up beneath his arm, the other foot dangling just above the water. He was lip reading again. It wasn't difficult — survivors in distress had a limited vocabulary, and the body language filled in most of the gaps the distance created. David was swearing at the door. Leon was suggesting something David didn't want to hear. Jake was agreeing with Leon, which David also didn't want to hear. Standard. He stifled a yawn behind his mask. Since the basement rescue, the group had consolidated into something almost boring — five people moving with grim shared purpose toward a goal that wasn't going to cooperate with them, working a door that had made its position clear approximately twenty minutes ago. Competent enough, under the circumstances. Dull to watch. The basement had been genuinely entertaining. The pipe hallway had been a masterpiece. This was just attrition dressed up as effort, and he'd filmed enough of it already. "Come on, guys. Give me something dramatic." He shifted his weight on the cabinet and waited for something to happen. The lens swept across the group and snagged on Dwight. He'd been tracking the door crew on autopilot, but Dwight pulled his focus back. Something was just slightly wrong about the quality of his stillness. He wasn't watching the door. Wasn't watching the water. Just standing against the wall with his palm flat to the plaster and his lips moving in something too small and too steady to be talking to anyone. His eyes kept moving across the group in that particular way — not checking on them, not looking for reassurance. He almost seemed to be counting. “Ooo what have we here? Do I sense a crack in the resolve?” Danny watched him through the green-tinted lens and felt something adjacent to pity. The man had been dunked twice, dragged through a flooded maze in the dark, and was now standing hip-deep in whatever this building was turning into, quietly coming apart over what looked like an arithmetic problem. Bless. The twitchy ones always found something to fixate on when the adrenaline ran out of places to go. Numbers, patterns, routines — anything the brain could chew on to avoid sitting with the actual situation. He'd seen it before. He'd filmed it before. He zoomed in, tracking the shape of his muttering as he whispered, “Five... why are there five people? It’s never an odd number!” Danny chuckled softly, rolling his eyes and rapping the butt of his knife softly against the cabinet’s side in idle rhythm while zooming back in on the futile struggle at the door. “Guy is losing it. Already spiraling in on himself and obsessing over nothing. He's not even helping them anymore. Oh nooo an odd number in the school! Honestly, if he’s so upset about the numbers, he can chill. I’m here too. Nice even six. Better?” The sarcasm landed hollow. He chuckled anyway. The amusement faded a little faster than it should have. Danny tapped the hilt of his knife against the cabinet edge, a slow idle rhythm, and watched Dwight count his people for what was probably the fourth time. The motion settled him, usually — something to do with his hands while his brain ran wherever it wanted to go. It wasn't settling him now. There was something sitting at the back of his thoughts that hadn't been there thirty seconds ago, shapeless and faintly irritating. He turned his attention back to the door crew and let it sit. Clearly the man was cracking. Two trips through a flooded maze in pitch dark would do that to anyone, and Dwight had never been what you'd call a stable baseline to begin with. Twitchy. Overthought everything. The kind of person who needed the rules to make sense or the whole framework started wobbling. Made him a decent leader in a normal trial — pattern recognition, steady under pressure, knew the rhythm of things — and made him exactly this in a trial that had stopped following rules an hour ago. The odd number was probably just a loose thread his brain had found and couldn't stop pulling. The knife hilt rapped softly. Once. Twice. Although... She did love her rituals. That was just true. The whole apparatus of a trial ran on repetition, on symmetry, on the same beats landing in the same order often enough that it bordered on obsession. He'd run more trials than he could count and the numbers never varied, not once, not even when everything else about a domain went sideways. The structure held because the structure was the point. This whole night had been a weird flex on Her part. The flooding alone was unusual — theatrical, expensive, not Her typical economy of effort. She fed on fear, not spectacle. Spectacle was a means to an end and usually a fairly efficient one, not a whole elaborate aquarium with rising water and geometry that kept rewriting itself. That was a lot of energy for one trial. More than made sense. And She'd done it with five people. Danny stopped tapping. He looked at the group again — not through the lens, just looked, the phone dropping slightly in his hand. Five people at a door that wasn't opening, in a building that was doing something sustained and deliberate and costly, and She had set all of it in motion with a number that didn't fit Her own ritual logic. Fuck. He's starting to sound like them. Maybe the mold in the air was getting to him too. This place had been wet for hours and he'd been breathing whatever was in the air the same as everyone else, and it was apparently doing something to his higher functions. He exhaled through his nose and directed his attention firmly back to the door. The thought sat there anyway, refusing to fade off. He shifted on the cabinet, crossing his legs and rolling his shoulders against the pull of the leather. The shoulder pads creaked quietly in protest, the leather of the robe sticking slightly with each motion, heavier than usual. Weighted. Trapping warmth instead of wicking it off like normal. He winced. The outfit was fantastic for blending in with the shadows, both flexible and breathable, but it was heavy at the best of times. Right now, it sat heavier on him than he remembered. Every seam had absorbed something. The underlayer clung. He'd been carrying the extra weight long enough that he'd stopped registering it consciously, which probably explained why his back had opinions that it was only now getting around to voicing. He'd peel it off later, hang it up, let it dry properly. Later problem. He glanced down at his phone, adjusting his grip, and the faint glow of the screen caught the air around his hands. No fog. Not the building's water-thick atmosphere — that was everywhere, unavoidable, a permanent feature of the evening. His fog. The particular dark that clung to him when he didn't want to be seen, that softened his edges and swallowed his silhouette and had been as automatic as breathing since the first trial. It was just there. It was always just there. He turned his hand over slowly in the phone's light. Nothing. Just his hand. Just air. No shimmer of stealth, no ripple of distortion, no indication he had been cloaked at all, really. And come to think of it... he had no idea how long he’d even been fully visible for. Had he been uncloaked this whole time? He looked up at the group — really looked, the lens forgotten — and did the math with the particular speed of someone who had spent years reading rooms for a living. Orela's flashlight had swept this hallway. Multiple times. He'd been sitting on a toppled cabinet in the open, phone out, knife visible, not eight meters away, and not one of them had so much as flinched in his direction. “...Huh.” How did the others not feel him there? Was his terror radius even active? He reached inward for the low constant pulse of it, the thing that kept prey at the right edge of awareness. The thing that had always been there. The silence where it should have been was very loud. Across the hallway, Dwight was still against his wall. Still counting. Still wearing that expression — hollowed out, fraying at the edges, the look of someone standing at the threshold of understanding something they didn't want to understand. Danny looked at him for a long moment. No stealth. No presence. No terror radius. “...Wait.” The school flinched inward. All at once, simultaneously, every seam in the building giving up the pretense at the same moment — as if it had been holding its breath since the trial started and had finally, finally found its cue. The pipes went first. Not a chain reaction building from a source — all of them, the entire network detonating in the same instant with a shriek of pressure that compressed the air and hit the ears like a physical thing. Locker doors flew open along the hallway's length, torn off their hinges by the force of what came through them, water exploding outward in solid jets that crossed the corridor and hit the opposite wall hard enough to strip paint. Some doors didn't open at all — they shattered, the metal folding outward in jagged petals as the water behind them stopped asking permission. Ceiling tiles buckled and dropped, each one releasing its own small waterfall that joined the roar before it hit the floor, the sound building on itself until it stopped being individual sources and became a single deafening presence that swallowed everything inside it. The surge scattered the survivors across the flooded foyer, drowning out their yells beneath its violent crescendo, consuming the survivor’s panicked screaming shouts, and dousing them in spray from all sides. Orela's flashlight became a liability. The beam swung wild as the first jets hit — catching nothing useful, just strobing across walls and water and the shapes of people staggering, the light more disorienting than the dark had been. She swept it hard left, trying to find something solid to orient by, and a pressure wave caught her from the right and took her feet. The beam lurched toward the ceiling. Her shoulder hit something — a locker, a wall, she couldn't tell — before Leon's arm came across her chest and pulled, hauling her back against him and turning his body into a windbreak between her and the spray. She got a hand against the wall. Held. Across the foyer, Jake moved on reflex. He'd seen Dwight's legs go the instant the first wave hit — no purchase, no warning, just a man with too much height and not enough weight suddenly at the mercy of a current that had been waiting for exactly this. Jake was already moving when Dwight started to go down, closing the distance in two lurching strides, catching him by the arm and driving him hard into the nearest corner. He planted himself between Dwight and the worst of it, braced wide, and held. At the door, David had nowhere to go. The door was at his back — immovable, indifferent, the same door that had absorbed everything they'd thrown at it all night — and the water was at his front, coming in from three directions at once. He got his arm up, elbow leading, and turned his face into his shoulder as a jet caught him across the chest and drove the breath out of him. The force of it ground him back against the wood. He pushed into it, found his footing, lost it, found it again. Another wave hit, lower, and the cold of it surged up his torso. He coughed hard into his own arm and kept his feet. Down the hall, Danny was torn loose. No warning, no build — one moment he was sitting upright
